data.title: Asian shares find footing after bruising month; US dollar set for third monthly gain
data.description:
SYDNEY – Asian shares were set to end a bruising month on a steadier note as a holiday lull offered some respite from AI jitters, while the US dollar reigned supreme, riding a wave of safe-haven demand and rate hike bets towards a third month of gains.

Oil prices were headed for the first weekly rise in four on renewed concerns about supply disruptions. Brent crude futures slipped 0.4% on Nov 27 to US$96.14 a barrel, but were still up 3.9% for the week. For November, they were down 18%.

Wall Street was closed on Nov 26 for the Thanksgiving holiday, but in Asia, S&P 500 futures were up 0.8% and Nasdaq futures were 1% higher.

Japan’s Nikkei rose 0.7% to bring its gains for the week to 2.7%, clawing back only a fraction of its 8.4% loss for November.

Data showed on Nov 27 that core inflation in Tokyo hit a 16-month high in November, bolstering the case for an interest rate hike from the Bank of Japan as soon as December.

MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan edged up 0.5% to end the week 1.9% higher. It was still down 8.2% for November.

Shares in South Korea rallied 2% and China’s blue chips slipped 0.2%, after hitting the lowest level since June 2025 on Nov 26.

“Barring a big shock that severely rattles a thin market, November is practically in the books and the markets limp into December where a seasonal ‘Santa Rally’ currently appears elusive,” said Kyle Rodda, a senior analyst at Capital.com

“For as long as the markets remain unsure about the growth trajectory for AI and lack clarity about where US rates may peak, uncertainty and therefore volatility is liable to remain elevated.”

Tech giant Nvidia remained a source of unease after S&P put its credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade.

The chipmaker told manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers containing its chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, the Financial Times reported.

Elsewhere in tech, Elon Musk said that every child in the US would receive two shares in his space and AI company SpaceX, pledging a gift worth about US$18 billion (S$23.2 billion).

US dollar reigns

The US dollar was headed to its third monthly gain on Nov 27, up 1.8% against its major peers at 103.8. It has been supported by expectations that the Federal Reserve is almost certain to lift interest rates in December, as well as safe-haven flows from the selloff in equities.

Futures imply a 99% chance the Fed will raise rates by 25 basis points in December, but speculation of a half-point increase has faded.

The euro was last flat at US$1.0964, after news that Spanish central banking veteran Pablo Hernández de Cos would become the next European Central Bank president, a move that was well telegraphed and suggested policy continuity.

The kiwi edged up 0.2% to US$0.5482 after New Zealand’s ruling centre-right coalition fell short of a parliamentary majority, leaving it reliant on negotiations with the centrist Opportunity Party to stay in power.

Bond investors are wondering if the broad losses in global stocks in November coupled with doubts about the durability of AI-driven business investment might temper the hawkishness of central banks.

“The Fed could, of course, still blink,” said David Rees, chief economist at Schroders. “But a Fed put would not necessarily be unambiguously positive for markets.”

“If growth and inflation data remain firm, in a game of cat and mouse markets could soon begin pricing a more hawkish Fed back in, potentially setting off the same chain of events all over again.”

Two-year Treasury yields rose 3 basis points to 4.6705% as the cash market reopened after the US holiday. They were up 6 bps this week.

Benchmark 10-year Treasury yields rose 4 bps to 4.8918%, but were down 2 bps for the week. REUTERS

data.title: Tokyo’s faster pace of inflation backs case for Bank of Japan rate hike
data.description:
Inflation in Japan’s capital city accelerated to the fastest pace in 2026, backing the case for a Bank of Japan (BOJ) rate increase in December as authorities focus on keeping price growth around their 2% target.

The consumer price index excluding fresh food rose 2.9% in November from 2025 in Tokyo, the highest level since July 2025, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications reported on Nov 27. The result matched economists’ consensus forecast.

Tokyo inflation is a leading indicator of nationwide price trends. The index that strips out both fresh food and energy – a gauge closely monitored by the BOJ as a measure of underlying inflation – climbed 2.5%, while overall CPI rose 2.8%.

Among the factors driving gains were rising costs for electricity, up 9.5%, and for city gas bills, which increased by almost 14%.

In both cases, the figures reflect the impact of the end of subsidies on utility bills that Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s government rolled out for three months in the summer. Price gains for processed food also accelerated.

“The impact of the end of utility measures was the biggest force for the core CPI to rise,” said Yoshiki Shinke, senior executive economist at Daiichi Life Research Institute.

“It’s still safe to say the data show businesses have a strong desire to pass their heightened costs to consumers, given price pressures stemming from the Middle East conflict and AI demand.”

Rice prices dropped almost 34%, the biggest decline in the data going back to 1971. Rice, a daily staple for households, has become a major drag on CPI after being among the primary drivers of overall inflation in 2025.

The Nov 27 CPI data generally back the case for the BOJ to raise interest rates in December.

The central bank judged in October that underlying inflation had reached a level broadly consistent with its 2% target, shifting its focus toward keeping price growth anchored around that level after previously focusing on coaxing the price trend higher.

“The assessment that upside risks to inflation remain high hasn’t changed, so there is a strong likelihood of a rate hike in December,” said Nomura Securities economist Uichiro Nozaki.

Economist Taro Kimura from Bloomberg Economics said: “We maintain our baseline call for a 25-basis-point rate hike in December. But, against the backdrop of recent stock-market turbulence, the CPI report argues for caution on rapid tightening. A December move remains a close call.”

Service prices – a key measure of the sustainability of inflation – increased 2.1% from 2025, largely unchanged.

Takaichi in October announced plans to reinstate utility subsidies for three months starting in December.

She is also seeking to cut the sales tax on food from April 2027 to ease the cost-of-living burden on households. At the same time, the government will scale back gasoline subsidies. Together, those measures complicate the BOJ’s task of gauging underlying inflation.

Earlier this week, the BOJ’s consumer price indicator that subtracts the impact of temporary government steps accelerated in October to 3.5%, the fastest pace in three years. Service prices charged among businesses also rose by the most in 36 years.

Unlike the era of prolonged deflation, Japanese businesses have been quick to reflect their rising costs stemming from the Middle East conflict.

Major food and beverage companies were planning to raise the prices of 1,477 products in November, almost ten times more than a year ago, according to Teikoku Databank.

While real wages have risen every month in 2026, consumer spending has remained sluggish, contracting for two consecutive quarters through September. The government downgraded its assessment of consumption this week.

BOJ governor Kazuo Ueda has pledged to monitor the economy, inflation and financial conditions in determining the timing of rate moves.

The BOJ delivers its next decision on Dec 18. The governor is scheduled to deliver a speech on Nov 30 in which he may offer hints regarding December’s meeting. BLOOMBERG

data.title: HSBC reorganises India support roles, impacting hundreds of jobs
data.description:
HSBC Holdings is consolidating some support functions in India as the Asia-focused lender steps up efforts to rein in costs and accelerate the adoption of artificial intelligence. 

The bank recently told employees in India that it was centralising finance functions across cities including Chennai, Gurugram and Bangalore, and will no longer be housing those roles in other hubs, including Hyderabad and Pune, according to people with knowledge of the matter, who requested not to be named because the information is private.

The changes are confined to finance roles within HSBC’s so-called global capability centres in India, and employees expect the move to affect several hundred roles, according to the people.

HSBC staff will be given the option and support to relocate, but the bank will not provide further cash incentives for them to move, the people added.

HSBC has been weighing deep job cuts over the coming years as chief executive Georges Elhedery deploys AI to shrink its middle and back offices.

Non-client facing roles in global service centres are among those expected to be most impacted, people familiar have said previously. The changes could ultimately impact around 20,000 roles, or about 10% of its total workforce.

“As we simplify the bank, our focus remains on ensuring we have the right roles in the right locations to support the best customer outcomes,” an HSBC spokesperson said in a statement, referring to the roles in India.

“We are taking the best of our people experience and combining this with emerging technologies to deliver outcomes that are better, faster and safer for our clients.”

India has emerged as a key market for HSBC, alongside other major banks. HSBC describes itself as the largest foreign lender in the country and generated US$1.9 billion (S$2.45 billion) of pre-tax profit in the region in 2025.

It had about 47,000 employees in India at the end of 2025. About 42,500 employees work in the global capability centres in India, including on technology, according to estimates from a person familiar with the matter.

Other banks have also been reshaping their Indian hubs, which have grown so large that Goldman Sachs Group and JPMorgan employ more people in India than anywhere else outside the US.

They are using AI to automate work such as checking loan documents, reconciling accounts and writing basic code, the same tasks that once gave fresh graduates their first jobs at those centres. 

Lenders globally are expecting AI to lead to fewer roles in the future. Standard Chartered plans to cut close to 8,000 support roles over four years, while JPMorgan Chase & Co chief executive Jamie Dimon has said the technology will eliminate jobs broadly across industries.

Banks are trimming junior analyst classes by as much as two-thirds, Debasish Patnaik, a senior partner at McKinsey & Co, said in June.

At HSBC, Elhedery has accelerated an overhaul of Europe’s largest bank through asset sales and operational simplification. 

In August, the lender said it expects its global restructuring effort to yield US$2 billion in cost savings, up from an earlier target of US$1.5 billion.

The banker has made streamlining HSBC a central principle, saying earlier in 2026 that he had been “ruthless about killing complexity” at the lender. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Black Friday? No thanks, some brands say
data.description:
LONDON/MILAN/LOS ANGELES – While most brands are dangling deep Black Friday discounts to entice shoppers, some are opting out. These holdouts want to protect profits, make a point about sustainability, or simply stand out and try to connect with a growing number of consumers wary of permanent promotions.

In Italy, fashion brand Pinko is for the first time sitting out Black Friday in 2026, with chairman Pietro Negra saying discounting can become a vicious cycle.

“By not taking part in Black Friday, we’re trying to cut off one small head of a dragon that has another thousand,” said Negra, pointing to “family and friends” promotions, private sales and other events that encourage discounting.

“That’s not the kind of relationship we want with customers, nor are those the conditions that will secure the future of the sector.”

Retailers around the world have had a challenging year with the Iran war reigniting inflation and cash-strapped consumers needing sizeable discounts to be swayed into buying.

But while giants like Amazon can afford to slash prices as they hoover up most Black Friday traffic, the discount frenzy can be a double-edged sword for small brands, impacting profitability and making shoppers less willing to pay full-price the rest of the time.

Negra said not participating in Black Friday will cost Pinko around €2 million (S$2.83 million) in revenue, but the hit to profitability is proportionally much smaller, and margin is what he is focused on.

Fighting discount fatigue

After five years of persistently high inflation, shoppers are increasingly sceptical of retailers’ pricing strategies and less likely to believe that advertised discounts reflect real savings, said Shikha Jain, a partner at Simon-Kucher consultancy in Boston.

Choosing not to embrace Black Friday is risky, as competition for every dollar is fierce. But choosing to opt out may give brands a different kind of visibility and help them build trust, especially among less price-sensitive shoppers.

“There has been a serious erosion of trust,” said Jain, adding that she sees “increasing pullback, and major fatigue against inflation and the challenging environment that many Americans find themselves in”.

Brands that opt out are also angling for a slice of consumers’ attention even if it doesn’t translate into sales instantly, instilling a message or winning brownie points.

British outerwear brand Buffalo Systems says it does not participate in Black Friday because it is a small business manufacturing in Britain, while American outdoor retailer REI closes its stores on Black Friday and gives employees a day off to spend outside instead.

The Ordinary, a skincare brand owned by beauty giant Estee Lauder, also shuts its stores for the day and runs blood donation drives in New York and Toronto instead.

Amy Bi, senior vice-president of global brand at The Ordinary, said impulse-buying around Black Friday often leads to people buying products they do not need or that are not right for their skin, and halting sales for the day is a way of encouraging consumers to “slow down”.

Anti-Black Friday marketing

Smaller brands may be less able to sacrifice the much-needed sales boost Black Friday provides, and are instead leaning into a contrarian kind of marketing to set themselves apart.

UpCircle, a British beauty brand that uses coffee grounds, oat husks and other food industry by-products to make its creams and scrubs, runs its own Black Friday discounts while promoting its anti-waste ethos in Instagram posts that criticise overproduction and overconsumption, using social media slang like “landfill maxxing”.

Black Friday was popularised in the US but has gone global since the early 2000s, driven partly by Amazon and other multinational retailers.

Black Friday is “the antithesis of everything we stand for when it comes to the associations with waste, with mass consumption”, said UpCircle founder Anna Brightman.

But its anti-consumerist posts attract eyeballs in a highly competitive market, Brightman said, and the 25% discount across the range helps convince new customers to try their first product. In just three weeks around Black Friday, Upcircle makes 20% of its online sales for the year. REUTERS

data.title: Asian stocks stabilise after tech rout
data.description:
HONG KONG – Asian stocks stabilised on Nov 26 from another hard day of selling as the tech sector enjoyed a much-needed bounce, while investors took in their stride a fresh round of proposed US tariffs.

The gains came after a dip-buying afternoon rally helped US markets finish well off their initial lows as Wall Street headed into the Thanksgiving holiday on an only slightly negative note.

Beaten-down Asian tech firms led the gains on Nov 26, with Seoul, Tokyo and Taipei again at the centre of the action, having seen wild swings this week amid concerns about the AI boom, while the euphoria over Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia has worn off.

Japanese chipmaker Kioxia was the standout, surging by double figures, while South Korean titan SK Hynix were also comfortably up.

Tokyo’s Nikkei 225, the Kospi in Seoul and the Taipei Taiex all advanced – even if they ended off their earlier highs – while the Hang Seng in Hong Kong climbed more than 1%. There were also gains in Sydney, Mumbai, Singapore and Jakarta. Shanghai was flat, while Bangkok, Wellington and Manila dipped.

London, Frankfurt and Paris opened sharply higher.

Global markets have whipsawed this week, with news of Huang’s return – despite an affair with an alleged Chinese spy – lighting up Asian screens on Nov 24 before a crushing drop on Nov 25.

After a stellar start to 2026, selling in the past five months has been fanned by fears over vast capital expenditure and when that will pay off, as well as rising interest rate expectations and talk of tighter AI regulation under a new Democrat-led Congress.

Some observers have said there were signs the pain could be nearing its end.

But Michael Boutros at Forex.com warned that “buyers still need to demonstrate that renewed demand extends beyond short-lived relief rallies”.

“The focus heading into December is on whether semiconductor shares can regain traction and support a broader recovery or whether the recent deterioration signals further downside.”

And analysts at Manulife said in a note: “The market rebound is encouraging, but it should not be interpreted as confirmation that the period of volatility has ended.

“Following a sharp sell-off and increasingly oversold market conditions, further near-term gains are possible. Nevertheless, investors should be prepared for additional swings.”

Expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike in December were given a fresh boost on Nov 25 by data showing US inflation in October at a three-year high, while economic growth for the third quarter was revised upwards.

There was little movement in reaction to the unveiling of proposed US tariffs on 14 economies following a months-long probe into alleged excess production.

The duties of up to 20% face a period of public comment before taking effect, with an official adding that the proposals take existing trade deals into account.

The new levies target some of the largest US trading partners, including the European Union, India, Japan and South Korea.

China faces a 20% toll, the joint-highest for any economy, but US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new levies were within the bounds of existing trade negotiations with Beijing.

Beijing warned Washington not to engage in “tariff wars and trade wars”. AFP

data.title: SAP weighs cutting at least 10,000 positions in AI restructuring
data.description:
SAP is preparing a plan to eliminate at least 10,000 positions to transform its software business for the artificial intelligence era, according to people familiar with the matter. 

The restructuring would affect at least 9% of the global workforce, the people said, asking not to be identified because discussions are ongoing. The total number of job cuts hasn’t been finalised and might still change after labour negotiations, they added. 

The plans come after SAP, Europe’s most valuable software company, reorganised its executive board twice in 2026 as part of a push by Chief Executive Officer Christian Klein to promote an AI-first strategy. Two of six board members will leave the Walldorf, Germany-based company in March. 

“SAP continuously reviews its organisation to ensure it remains aligned with its strategy and customer needs,” the company said in a statement, declining to comment on whether any job cuts are planned. 

As part of the changes, SAP’s leadership will continue to redesign how it develops and sells products, according to the people. Klein is seeking to embed AI tools into the company’s applications, after earlier attempts to introduce AI products faced problems.

All departments are being asked to identify areas for potential cuts, with product and engineering and sales departments in particular focus, according to the people. 

Klein took over most of the responsibilities of product lead Muhammad Alam in 2026 after he didn’t renew his contract, which ends in March. Sales chief Thomas Saueressig, who had been given an expanded role earlier in 2026, said last week he will leave the company to become CEO of Ionos Group SE. 

SAP historically has announced major restructurings in late January alongside its full-year results, most recently in 2024. Around 10,000 positions were eliminated in that effort, which cost around €3 billion (S$4.25 billion) and took over a year. It was mainly handled through voluntary departures and retraining workers, with the total number of employees remaining relatively flat as SAP hired for new positions. 

In Germany, where SAP has the largest number of employees, the labour council in 2026 negotiated an employment guarantee through 2028. SAP employs more than 110,000 people worldwide.

“Our headcount has increased a little bit over the course of the year,” Chief Financial Officer Dominik Asam said at a Morgan Stanley conference last week, adding he “would be really surprised” if that trend didn’t reverse. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Indonesian nickel tycoon Arif Kurniawan named suspect in money laundering probe
data.description:
NEW YORK – The Indonesian attorney general’s office has named nickel trader Arif Kurniawan as a suspect in a money laundering case, after warning of irregularities in his business dealings earlier in November.

Kurniawan allegedly laundered proceeds from illegal mining and concealed the funds through intermediaries and affiliate firms between 2021 and 2026, the AGO said in a statement late on Nov 25.

The well-known trader was named in the statement only by his initials, although his identity was confirmed by authorities earlier in November.

Kurniawan denied any wrongdoing and rejected the allegations when contacted by Bloomberg News, saying all of his previous trading activities had complied with relevant laws and regulations.

Investigators have seized documents and more than US$3 million (S$3.9 million) in cash in various currencies, as well as almost 38kg of gold bars, in relation to the case, the AGO said.

A reclusive but important figure in Indonesia’s mining industry, Kurniawan has risen rapidly since leaving Glencore more than a decade ago to become the country’s top nickel ore trader.

The targeting of his sprawling mining and trading business could trigger a shake up of the wider sector, in a nation that accounts for about 60% of global supply.

Kurniawan is suspected to be outside of Indonesia, a spokesperson for the AGO said at a press conference earlier in November.

In 2024, he traded about a third of the country’s nickel ore supply, Bloomberg reported in 2025, citing a survey of industry figures. Alongside a business partner, Kurniawan also had stakes in at least 20 mining concessions spread across Indonesia. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Billions in data centre deals grind to halt after AI chip curbs
data.description:
Lenders have hit the brakes on billions of dollars in loans tied to Chinese firms ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent, as new US curbs on chip access threaten to upend Asia’s burgeoning AI debt financing market. 

While Jensen Huang’s surprise return to Nvidia buoyed AI stocks briefly earlier this week, bankers remained concerned about the legal risks of financing data centres and neoclouds potentially facing stricter US export controls.

Deals that were near the finish line are suddenly in doubt and lenders trying to sell down their exposure are struggling to find interested buyers.

Some lenders have delayed moving forward as they do more due diligence on an upsized US$6.6 billion (S$8.51 billion) loan sought by Bain Capital’s Bridge Data Centres (BDC), whose Malaysian facilities are used by clients including ByteDance, according to people involved in the discussions.

Bain referred questions to BDC, which declined to comment. ByteDance did not respond to a request for comment. 

One bank has decided to pass on a fully underwritten US$372 million loan for Partners Group-backed Digital Halo, while others are asking more questions, people familiar with those talks said.

The funds are for a data centre in Malaysia that services Alibaba and other customers, they said. Multiple banks were also reassessing a US$480 million loan for Aolani, a Singapore-based neocloud that gets business from ByteDance, separate people familiar with the matter said last week.

The companies all either did not respond to questions or declined to comment.

The Biden administration’s 2022 export restrictions on advanced US chips spawned an ecosystem of companies in South-east Asia to help Chinese technology firms access the coveted hardware remotely.

Lending to data centres in the region surged in the following years, while chip financing was just beginning to take off more recently as banks got more comfortable with the riskier deals.

That changed after the US announced last week that companies in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil will need a US government licence to purchase advanced AI chips from American manufacturers.

Globally, data centres that already lease significant compute to Chinese firms will need a separate licence to continue doing so, and have a 90-day window to obtain it.

More than a dozen bankers said their teams were waiting for answers on how the new curbs would affect borrowers and that would at the very least delay potential deals from going through.

Lenders including Citigroup and Standard Chartered, as well as Singapore’s major banks, have launched a sweeping review of data centre clients, people familiar with the matter said earlier. 

Some banks are looking to reduce certain exposure to AI and data centre debt, including through secondary loan sales and so-called significant risk transfers (SRTs).

Singapore’s United Overseas Bank is seeking an SRT deal of around US$1 billion to offload risks tied to data centre and infrastructure loans among other sectors, people familiar with the matter said. But the current news headlines are slowing progress, one of them said, adding that details are not firmed up and could change.

A representative for UOB declined to comment, citing deal confidentiality. 

Private lenders, who were the most aggressive in seeking out the higher returns associated with GPU financing, are also growing more cautious.

At least one fund has decided not to participate in a US$300 million loan to GMI Cloud, an Nvidia cloud partner, to fund chips for a Thai data centre that would be used by Tencent, according to a person familiar with the matter.

GMI Cloud and Tencent did not respond to requests for comment. 

The chill has extended beyond debt financing. DayOne Data Centers, whose biggest customer is ByteDance, has put plans for a US public listing on hold, people familiar with the matter said earlier. A consortium involving BlackRock is considering lowering its offer for a portfolio of Asia Pacific data centres, according to separate people familiar.

It is not a bad thing that the new restrictions have forced a broad re-evaluation of deals, according to Ben Kostrzewa, an international trade lawyer at Hogan Lovells Cadwalader.

Since 2023, loans to data centre companies in Asia-Pacific have soared from virtually zero to more than US$49 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

“It could be a good pause, to take stock and to review these projects, given how frothy the market has been for a while,” Kostrzewa said. “It won’t stop all these data centres being built, it won’t stop the market, but it will slow it all down.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: Nasdaq, S&P 500 end down, but well off lows as investors buy bargains
data.description:
NEW YORK – The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq retreated on Nov 25 amid a tech sell-off, but finished well off the day’s lows as bargain hunters stepped in ahead of the US Thanksgiving holiday.

The Dow finished higher.

The Nasdaq had been more than 4% lower earlier in the session as the sell-off in AI-related stocks and new US tariff proposals hit sentiment.

“There are all these potential headwinds, but then there’s also a certain amount of conditioning of buying on the dip, and that’s part of what we’re seeing,” said Oliver Pursche, senior vice-president and adviser for Wealthspire Advisors in Westport, Connecticut.

“The broad sell-offs tend to kind of throw the baby out with the bathwater. Investors are taking advantage of some of those discrepancies,” he said.

Technology led declines among S&P 500 sectors, while materials and real estate were among top sector gainers.

Wall Street has been roiled this month, partly because of worries about AI leader Nvidia. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO earlier in November, but the company’s board reinstated him on Nov 23. The S&P 500 is down roughly 5% for the month.

Volume was lower than average ahead of the holiday. The market will be closed on Nov 26 and will close early on Nov 27.

According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 18.01 points, or 0.25%, to end at 7,183.08 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 154.10 points, or 0.65%, to 23,579.44.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 155.20 points, or 0.31%, to 50,173.90.

AI worries weigh on market

Nvidia shares fell along with an index of semiconductors as the tech sell-off deepened.

Fears of increased regulatory scrutiny of the AI sector following the Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections have added to worries about AI stocks.

Early in the day, the Nasdaq 100 briefly fell 20% from its record closing high, flirting with bear-market territory.

Investors were also digesting news that the US proposed new tariffs on goods from 14 trading partners to combat what it calls structural excess industrial capacity, reviving global trade tensions.

Data showed the US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter, while inflation increased further in October, reinforcing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December and again in early 2027.

The extra tariffs could cloud the outlook for investors grappling with the prospect of interest rates staying higher for longer, as inflation has accelerated and oil prices have risen steadily due to the US-Iran war. REUTERS

data.title: Fraud, scam claims against S’pore financial firms rise for third year
data.description:
SINGAPORE – For the third year running, fraud and scam victims made up the largest group of consumers turning to the Financial Industry Disputes Resolution Centre (FIDReC) for help with disputes involving financial institutions, with claims averaging $24,531.

The centre received a record 5,344 claims against 103 financial organisations – including banks, insurers, investment firms and payment providers – in its financial year 2025/26 ended June 30. That is up 23% from 4,355 the previous year, it said in its annual report released on Nov 26.

Of these, 3,356 proceeded to dispute resolution proceedings, while 891 were resolved early by encouraging direct conversations between consumers and financial institutions.

The median claim amount rose to $5,655, up 16% from $4,859 the previous year, while the average claim amount rose 2% to $47,572.

FIDReC is an independent, non-profit centre that helps consumers resolve disputes with financial organisations through mediation and adjudication when they cannot settle the issues directly.

Fraud and scam claims made up 45% of the cases that proceeded to dispute resolution. FIDReC handled 1,515 such claims in FY2025/26 – an 18% rise from the 1,285 recorded in the previous year.

The centre also completed 1,523 fraud and scam-related claims during the year, up 64% from the year before. Of these, 63% of the consumers accepted settlement offers at mediation, while 27% chose not to continue after mediation.

Of the fresh fraud and scam claims in FY2025/26, 1,460 were against banks and finance companies, and 53 against payment service providers such as stored-value e-wallet providers.

The remaining two claims involved capital markets service licensees, which include brokerages and fund managers.

FIDReC said 54% of the fraud and scam claims handled involved compromised user credentials. 

In these instances, consumers discovered unauthorised transactions on their bank accounts, debit or credit cards or digital wallets, but could not identify how these transactions occurred. 

Impersonation (14%) and online purchase (10%) scams rounded out the top three scam types.

Larger losses to scams, more older victims

Across all fraud and scam cases, the median claim amount jumped from $4,175 to $5,000, an increase of 20% from FY2024/25. The average claim amount, however, fell 10% to $24,531.

This divergence between the average and median claim amounts suggests that while the typical consumer sought redress for larger losses than in the previous year, fewer outsized claims skewed the overall average upwards. 

Looking closer at the profile of the claimants, consumers aged 51 and above were the most affected, accounting for 53% of all scam-related claims, while cases involving claimants above 70 more than doubled from 59 to 130 cases. 

In one case, a 74-year-old woman transferred about $1.2 million over two weeks to a purported safe-keeping account after scammers posing as bank and government officials told her that she was being probed for money laundering.

She was told not to tell anyone about the confidential investigation, so when the bank queried the unusually large transfers, she repeated the scammers’ cover story, that she was buying another property.

The lady realised it was a scam only after the callers became uncontactable, and turned to FIDReC when the bank could not recover the funds.

At mediation, the bank maintained that she had authorised the transfers but offered a 10% goodwill settlement without admitting liability, which she accepted.

FIDRec highlighted the case to show how the circumstances of a scam can affect consumers’ claims for redress.

Eunice Chua, the centre’s chief executive, said that scammers are becoming more sophisticated, making it harder for consumers to realise they have been scammed. 

She added that rising scam-related disputes underscore the importance of prevention and access to a fair way to resolve them.

Chua suggested that consumers take proactive steps to protect themselves, such as using Money Lock, setting lower card limits and lowering thresholds for notification alerts.

She also urged them to remain vigilant and act immediately to prevent further losses if they suspect they are victims of a scam.

Claims up across the board

FIDReC said consumer claims rose across all categories in FY2025/2026.

The second-largest number of claims after fraud and scams related to the practices and policies of financial institutions, at 889, representing 26% of FIDReC’s caseload. 

These claims generally centre on contractual disputes, including disagreements over insurance policy terms such as exclusions, surrender values and payout conditions.

In one case, a consumer lost $5,000 after entering her card details and a one-time password on a phishing website while trying to make a purchase through TikTok. 

When she was unable to recover the money through her bank, she tried to make a claim under her scam cover insurance policy but was rejected by her insurer.

Her claim with FIDReC was dismissed at adjudication, as phishing websites were not covered by the policy, which covered only scams through specified channels, such as phone calls, e-mails or WhatsApp. 

FIDReC advised that consumers consider the risks they want protection against and ask the insurer whether those scenarios are included before buying insurance.

“A cyber insurance policy may not cover every type of scam. Read your policy carefully to understand what type of risks are covered.”

It further emphasised: “Insurance is not a substitute for staying alert to scams.”

FIDReC also handled 432 market conduct claims in FY2025/26. Such disputes typically involve giving inappropriate financial advice, making false and misleading statements about financial products, or inadequately disclosing information needed for customers to make decisions.

In one case, a woman in her early 40s invested most of her $200,000 savings in a fund that her financial adviser assured her over message was “principal guaranteed”.

When the fund failed and she could not recover her money, she filed a claim at FIDReC.

After mediation failed, the case proceeded to adjudication, which involves an independent, qualified professional appointed to hear the dispute and make a decision.

The financial institution argued that the policy documents the woman signed did not state that the principal was guaranteed.

The adjudicator, however, ruled in the woman’s favour – up to the $150,000 adjudication limit – finding that the company, through the financial adviser, had misrepresented the terms of the fund.

FIDReC said that the case underscores why consumers should scrutinise investment terms and risks, and they should also keep records – messages, e-mails and other communications – of what their financial adviser tells them.

Helping small businesses and charities

In FY2026, FIDReC extended its dispute resolution services to small businesses registered here with annual turnover of $1 million or under in each of the two preceding financial years, and registered charities with gross annual receipts below $10 million over the same period.

The take-up rate among small businesses was modest, with 17 claims handled. 

Of these, seven related to fraud and scams, six involved the practices and policies of financial institutions and four were over service standards, such as delays or errors in processing transactions or account updates. 

FIDReC said it will continue to raise awareness so small businesses and charities have an accessible way to resolve financial disputes.

data.title: Fewer people in S’pore changed jobs in 2026, but most who did earned more: MOM
data.description:
SINGAPORE - Fewer workers in Singapore are changing jobs as hiring slows and more seek job stability, even though those who switch employers are more likely to get a higher pay.

About two-thirds, or 65.6%, of full-time resident employees aged 25 to 64 who changed jobs saw their incomes rise after accounting for inflation, with most of these gains amounting to at least 5%.

The figures were released by the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) on Nov 27 in its annual labour force advance report.

The proportion of employed residents who changed jobs in the past year fell to 5.7% in 2026, extending the gradual downtrend from its peak in 2022.

The decline in job switching was most pronounced among younger residents aged below 30, particularly those aged 15 to 24. Younger workers who stayed in their jobs cited job stability as the most common reason for staying.

Meanwhile, older workers aged 50 and above were least likely to change jobs, with around half of older job stayers holding on to their current jobs for at least a decade.

MOM also tracked the longer-term income outcomes of workers who changed jobs, and found that they were more likely to enjoy real income gains than those who did not, director of MOM’s manpower research and statistics department Ang Boon Heng noted at a media briefing on Nov 27.

Job switchers were more likely than job stayers to see real income gains, with about 67% of them seeing higher incomes from 2025 to 2026, compared with around 61% who stayed in their jobs. The gap widens when looking at a five-year period from 2021 to 2026. For example, the older cohort who changed jobs in 2023 saw their incomes rise over a longer period following the job switch.

More than nine in 10 job switches over the past year were voluntary rather than due to retrenchments, said MOM.

Income outcomes were weaker in a small segment of workers who changed jobs involuntarily. Around 58% enjoyed wage income gains in their new jobs relative to their previous job, lower than the 67% recorded among voluntary job switchers.

While the majority of both groups saw higher incomes when they switched jobs, the ministry noted that involuntary job switchers were less likely to surpass earnings made in their old job.

Many job switchers moved across industries or occupations. Residents who changed industries typically remained in or moved into industries with above-average productivity, such as wholesale trade and financial and insurance services, while those who changed occupations commonly moved between PMET (professionals, managers, executives and technicians) jobs.

These cross-sector and cross-occupation transitions show how transferable skills and experience can support workers to navigate labour market changes, said MOM.

Job mobility continued to ease across most sectors, including professional services and financial and insurance services, partly reflecting softer hiring and business restructuring.

But information and communications sector showed an exception, with the share of employed residents who changed jobs edging up from 8.1% in 2025 to 8.7% in 2026. MOM said the increase indicates ongoing workforce reallocation efforts and changing skill needs as firms adapt to technological developments.

data.title: Real incomes in S’pore rise in 2026 but at slower pace, with smaller gains for lower-wage workers
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Workers in Singapore saw their incomes grow in 2026 but at a slower pace - after taking higher inflation into account.

Real median income of full-time employed residents rose by 2.2% in 2026, down from 4.1% in 2025.

For workers at the 20th percentile of the income distribution, real income growth slowed to 1.3%, from 3.6% the year before.

The figures are released by the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) on Nov 27 in its annual labour force advance report. They are preliminary as full-year inflation data is not yet available for 2026.

MOM said the slower growth partly reflected more cautious wage increases by firms and higher inflation. Consumer prices are projected to rise by around 2% in 2026, compared with 0.9% in 2025.

The ministry said despite the slower gains for lower-wage workers in 2026, their incomes have grown faster than those at the median over the recent five- and ten-year periods.

It added that they will continue to be supported by progressive wage measures.

Permanent jobs remain the norm

MOM noted that employment quality remained broadly stable even with softening manpower demand and continued external uncertainty.

Employees accounted for 88.2% of employed residents in 2026.

Among resident employees, 91% held permanent jobs, edging up from 90.8% in 2025.

The share of employees on fixed-term contracts remained stable at 7.1%, while casual or on-call employment declined further to 2%.

Over the decade, there was a shift among fixed-term contract employees towards longer contracts of at least a year, the ministry said.

Unemployment rates

While Singapore’s unemployment rate stay low overall, there were signs of greater pressure on workers in non-professional roles.

The unemployment rate among non-professionals, managers, executives and technicians (non-PMETs) rose from 2.8% in 2025 to 3.5% in 2026, returning to levels seen in 2023 and 2024.

In contrast, unemployment among PMETs remained broadly stable at 2.7%.

The long-term unemployment rate, which measures the proportion of workers that has been unemployed for at least 25 weeks, edged up to 0.7% for both groups.

Among non-PMETs, the increase was driven by workers aged 50 and above.

Residents in their 50s recorded the highest incidence of retrenchment, rising from 2.4 to 3.6 per 1,000 employees between the second quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026.

Their six-month re-entry rate was also consistently below the overall average.

MOM said at a briefing on Nov 27 that the increase in unemployment rate for non-PMETs can be attributed to difficulties faced by older non-PMETs in securing employment.

The hiring conditions in certain sectors also softened. The long-term unemployment rate in sectors more exposed to the global economy, such as manufacturing and wholesale trade, rose from 0.7 per cent in 2025 to a five-year high of 0.9 per cent in 2026.

Overqualification

As the Singapore workforce becomes increasingly educated, the share of resident workers in PMET jobs rose to 65.2%.

But the overqualification rate has declined for the third consecutive year from 19.4% in 2025 to 18.7% in 2026, while the involuntary overqualification rate remained low at 1.6%. The latter suggests that a few workers were in jobs below their qualifications because they could not find suitable alternatives, MOM said.

The profiles of the voluntarily and involuntarily overqualified were “broadly similar”, with about half of the tertiary-educated working as associate professionals and technicians at 47.7% and 50.8% respectively. This reflects younger workers taking up entry-level jobs to gain experience for higher-skilled jobs, MOM said.

Labour under-utilisation, which refers to the unemployed and under-employed, remained low at in 2026.

The number of discouraged workers, which refers to people who gave up on their job search, remained low at 7,100 or 0.3% of the resident labour force.

There’s a slight dip in the proportion of part-time workers who want to do additional work but are unable to find a job, with time-related under-employment rate declining from 1.9% in 2025 to 1.7% in 2026.

Ageing workforce

Singapore’s labour force participation rate eased further for the fifth consecutive year since 2021, but remains largely stable despite its ageing population, hovering at 67.9% in 2025 and 67.8% in 2026.

Higher participation among women has helped to offset some of the pressures of an ageing population.

The rose across most five-year age groups, with larger increases among seniors.

Coupled with seniors’ growing share in the population, the proportion of residents aged 60 years and over in the labour force rose from 13.1% in 2016 to 19.5% in 2026.

Singapore’s labour force participation rate also remained among the highest – ranking 7th across Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development countries – ahead of countries such as Switzerland, Estonia, and Australia, MOM noted.

The findings in the advance labour force report were drawn from the annual Comprehensive Labour Force Survey, which covers a representative sample of 33,000 households. A total of 27,292 households responded to the survey conducted between March to July.

data.title: Over $9 billion of S’pore goods affected by US tariffs; trade deal will involve compromises: DPM Gan
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Singapore will continue to negotiate with the United States on lowering tariffs that threaten to hit about $9.4 billion worth of the Republic’s domestic exports, said Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong, adding that any deal, however, will require some give and take.

The proposed new tariffs of up to 20% would raise the effective tariff rate on Singapore goods from 7.8% to 10.3%, said DPM Gan, who is also Minister of Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade).

Even so, Singapore will negotiate any trade pact with the country’s interests at the centre of the discussion, he told a media briefing on Nov 26.

“We also have to bear in mind that whatever agreement we arrive (at) and achieve in the US, there will be give and take. There will be compromises. There will be trade-offs that we need to be prepared to accept,” he added.

“So I think, in this process, it’s always important to remember that we will always be visible and always have Singapore’s interests at heart.”

The briefing was held a day after the US Trade Representative (USTR) proposed to impose tariffs of up to 20% on Singapore and 13 other trading partners under Section 301, accusing them of producing more goods than they would under normal, market-oriented conditions.

The duties could take effect in early 2027, though USTR Jamieson Greer offered to consider lowering the proposed rate to 10% if Singapore reaches an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART) with Washington.

While the new tariff will not be stacked upon the previously announced Section 301 tariffs of 12.5% related to forced labour concerns, without an ART the new tariff rate could reach up to 20%.

Gan said the Government is engaging local companies to understand and assess how to assist them.

He said he was surprised by the US trade office’s actions and report, which raised many sticking points with Singapore’s economy.

“I am very surprised that this has happened because this is not something that we expected from an important, major trading partner,” he said.

USTR targets industrial policies and CPF

Apart from the statement that announced the new tariff, the USTR also issued a 168-page investigation report listing and explaining US concerns that follow the investigation the agency started in March.

According to the USTR’s investigation report on Singapore’s industrial policies, the specific acts, policies and practices related to structural excess capacity and production include the Singapore Manufacturing 2030 plan and the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 plan, as well as financial support to the manufacturing sector and firms in the electronics and semiconductors, health and petrochemicals industries.

The report also cited the “encouragement of or failure to address foreign direct investments from non-market economies (NMEs), particularly China, which permits further development of structural excess capacity and production, and encouragement of or failure to address imports from NMEs, which enables Chinese firms to offload excess production”.

Singapore trade deal will involve compromises

Asked what deal can Singapore negotiate given that it already has a free trade agreement (FTA) with the US, Gan said: “It’s an open question because it’s really for us to discuss with the US to see what their concerns are.

“Whether in the process of discussion we will be able to address some of their concerns, and if we are able to do so, we hope we look forward to lower tariffs. It may not be... either 10% or 20%. It may be somewhere in between. And if we are able to arrive (at) some agreeable tariff together with the trade-offs that we have to accept, I think it’s something that will be a subject of negotiation moving forward.”

He said Singapore will be actively engaging the US administration over tariffs over the next couple of months.

Still, he said the high tariff rate and the scrutiny of Singapore’s economic policies in the USTR report were quite disappointing.

“Our bilateral relations are multi-faceted. It’s not just economics, but many other aspects as well. So I think we’ll continue to hope to be able to continue to strengthen our bilateral relationship and look forward to looking for a way to resolve differences in our tariffs and our trade relationship, and to seek better tariff for our exporters.”

The USTR report also targeted Singapore’s Central Provident Fund (CPF), a social security mechanism for retirement savings, saying the Republic uses it to promote savings and depresses consumption to boost its current account surplus.

A current account surplus occurs when a country earns more from international transactions – such as exporting goods and services, collecting investment income abroad, and receiving transfers – than it pays out to the rest of the world over a given period.

Gan said: “It will be important for us to communicate with them to explain our position to them, and we hope that they will understand what CPF is about. It’s not a scheme to suppress consumption.”

The USTR also deemed several financial support schemes for Singapore firms and the agreement with Malaysia on the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone as government interventions that promote structural excess capacity and production.

Business community weighs in

The Singapore Business Federation (SBF) is disappointed by the USTR’s determination that Singapore’s policies and practices contribute to structural excess manufacturing capacity and burden US commerce.

“We do not believe the findings accurately reflect Singapore’s market-driven economy, our role as a global trading and logistics hub, or the mutually beneficial nature of US-Singapore economic relations,” said the country’s top trade body.

SBF said the impact of the new tariff on Singapore businesses will depend on the final US action, including the products covered, tariff rates, implementation timeline, and how any new tariffs interact with existing measures.

SBF chief executive officer Kok Ping Soon said the immediate priority is to help businesses navigate these uncertainties and remain competitive.

“SBF will work closely with the business community and the Government to understand the implications and shape the necessary support,” he said.

Singapore and the US inked an FTA in 2003. In 2024, the US’ overall trade surplus with the Republic amounted to US$27 billion (S$34.8 billion). In 2025, this trade surplus with Singapore grew to US$33 billion.

However, the USTR report states: “Although Singapore has run a sizeable bilateral goods trade deficit with the United States for nearly all of the past decade, this does not outweigh the negative effects of Singapore’s outsized manufacturing sector and comparatively low consumption.”

Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at Singapore-based independent think-tank Hinrich Foundation, said if the two sides enter talks for a new deal, the US will likely demand three things: substantial new investments in the US; commitments to curb the flow of “non-market economy” (the US’ code for China) involvement in Singapore-to-US trade; and digital trade commitments that keep Singapore aligned with the US and American companies and platforms.

“Singapore will have to decide if these new commitments are worthwhile,” Elms added.

Singapore, despite its small size, is the third-largest Asian investor in the US, behind Japan and South Korea. Bilateral trade and Singapore investments in the US support some 350,000 American jobs.

About 6,600 US companies are based in Singapore, while more than 250 Singapore companies operate across 45 US states, in sectors from logistics and agribusiness to aerospace and shipbuilding.

The USTR investigation into structural excess industrial capacity that is flooding world markets with cheap exports was conducted against a total of 16 US trading partners, including Washington’s close allies Japan, the European Union (EU) and South Korea.

The USTR has not proposed tariffs on goods from Mexico and Norway at the moment.

The affected trading partners other than Singapore are China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the EU, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

Some Singapore exports are also subject to US sectoral tariffs – with rates ranging from 25% to 50% – on steel, aluminium, copper and automotive parts.

data.title: US leaves door open to lower Singapore tariff deal even as it proposes 20% levy
data.description:
SINGAPORE – The United States has left the door open to a trade deal that could lower tariffs on Singapore goods, even as it proposed a new levy of up to 20% on the Republic and 13 other trading partners.

United States Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer offered to consider lowering the proposed rate in a Nov 25 (Washington time) statement, which accused the 14 trading partners of producing more goods than they would under normal, market-oriented conditions.

“The Trade Representative further proposes to consider adjusting the tariff rate applied to each good to 10% to account for any commitments in the event that Singapore were to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States or conclude other negotiations that are responsive to the determinations in this investigation into the acts, policies and practices of Singapore,” the Office of the USTR said.

Without such a deal, the proposed tariff rate under Section 301 could reach up to 20% and take effect in early 2027.

However, the actual burden would be lower than 20%, as the rate will be net of previously announced Section 301 tariffs of 12.5% related to forced labour concerns. The proposal is also subject to a comment and hearing process through January, which could change the outcome.

“The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies and practices includes to consider applying tariffs of up to 20%, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, on all goods of Singapore, with exemptions for certain goods,” the USTR statement added.

The USTR said it will accept requests to appear at the hearings, along with a summary of testimony by Jan 5, 2027. Written comments are due by that same date. USTR will hold hearings about the proposed actions in these investigations on Jan 25, 2027.

The US’ concerns are listed and explained at length in a separate 168-page USTR report that follows an investigation the agency started in March.

According to the USTR’s investigation report on Singapore’s industrial policies, the specific acts, policies and practices related to structural excess capacity and production include the Singapore Manufacturing 2030 plan and the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 (RIE2030) plan, as well as financial support to the manufacturing sector and firms in the electronics and semiconductors, health, and petrochemicals industries.  

The report also cited the “encouragement of or failure to address foreign direct investments from non-market economies (NMEs), particularly China, which permits further development of structural excess capacity and production, and encouragement of or failure to address imports from NMEs, which enables Chinese firms to offload excess production”.

Singapore’s Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry (METI) on Nov 26 expressed its disappointment over the new US tariffs, stating that the USTR’s probe leading to the proposed measure fails to take into account the unique structure of the Republic’s open, trade-reliant economy.

METI also said that Singapore “will continue to engage the USTR constructively, including to urge the USTR to reconsider its proposed actions on Singapore and to explore ways to reduce the tariff”.

However, it is still not clear if Singapore will negotiate an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART) with the US.

Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at Singapore-based independent think-tank Hinrich Foundation, said the ART had not been on the table for either side until now because for Washington, Singapore was that rare country with which it had a trade surplus and an existing bilateral free trade agreement.

Now, however, “the US has certainly made clear their interest in negotiating an ART”, she said.

She said if the two sides enter talks, the US will likely demand three things: substantial new investments in the US; commitments to curb the flow of “non-market economy” (the US’ code for China) involvement in Singapore-to-US trade; and digital trade commitments that keep Singapore aligned with the US and American companies and platforms.

“Singapore will have to decide if these new commitments are worthwhile,” Elms added.

In its engagements with Trump administration officials since 2025, Singapore has persistently denied that it enjoys a trade surplus with the US or that its exports to the world’s largest economy stem from any form of excess capacity.

In fact, the US has maintained a substantial trade surplus with Singapore for more than two decades. In 2025, that surplus exceeded US$33 billion (S$42 billion), according to METI.

Singapore, despite its small size, is the third-largest Asian investor in the US, behind Japan and South Korea. Bilateral trade and Singapore investments in the US support some 350,000 American jobs.

About 6,600 US companies are based in Singapore, while more than 250 Singapore companies operate in 45 US states in sectors from logistics to agribusiness, to aerospace and shipbuilding.

However, the USTR report states: “Although Singapore has run a sizeable bilateral goods trade deficit with the United States for nearly all of the past decade, this does not outweigh the negative effects of Singapore’s outsized manufacturing sector and comparatively low consumption.

“If Singapore did not have acts, policies and practices contributing to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing, then the United States would be able to export more goods to Singapore beyond those it currently exports. 

“Moreover, Singapore’s trade surplus with key trading partners captures potential market share from US exporters in other markets.”

Adjusting these policies and initiatives to the liking of the US will be as hard as, if not more difficult than, dealing with earlier US tariffs related to the alleged trade of goods associated with forced labour.

In September, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said in the context of those earlier tariffs that Singapore will continue to engage the US on lowering tariffs and help businesses and workers adapt, but will consider any steps carefully in response to the negotiations.

As a major trading hub with around $2.5 trillion in goods and services trade each year, including $1.4 trillion in goods, any US import restrictions would have significant implications for Singapore’s trade, Gan had said on Sept 8.

Tommy Koh, a Singaporean former diplomat and the chief negotiator for the US-Singapore free trade agreement (FTA) inked in 2003, remarked on the irony of the situation: “The US is giving Singapore a Thanksgiving present.”

In a social media post on Nov 26, he said there was no justification for the proposal because of the FTA between the two countries. “The US cannot impose tariffs on Singapore. It will be a violation of the agreement,” he said.

He added that the US also has a trade surplus with Singapore in services, and pointed out a Heritage Foundation study that found the Republic to be the most free economy in the world.

“We export to the world in sectors where we have a comparative advantage, and we import in sectors where we don’t. This is called international trade,” Koh said.

“I would like to remind my American friends that the US is the second-largest exporter in the world. The US exports energy, aerospace products, pharmaceutical products, electronics and agricultural products. Using its own criterion, can we say the US has a structural excess industrial capacity in these sectors?” he added.

The USTR investigation into structural excess industrial capacity that is flooding world markets with cheap exports was conducted against a total of 16 trading partners, including close allies Japan, the European Union and South Korea.

The USTR has not proposed tariffs on goods from Mexico and Norway at the moment.

Affected trading partners besides Singapore are China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the EU, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

Some Singapore exports are also subject to US sectoral tariffs – with rates ranging from 25% to 50% – on steel, aluminium, copper and automotive parts.

data.title: S&P warns Nvidia’s board may be compromised, puts chipmaker’s rating on downgrade watch
data.description:
S&P Global Ratings placed Nvidia’s credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade on Nov 25, saying the departure and subsequent reinstatement of its chief executive officer had exposed weaknesses in the chipmaker’s management and board oversight.

“We believe the long tenure of certain board members may have compromised their independence. The company’s corporate governance practices may also not have kept pace with Nvidia’s rapid growth and its role as a critical global technology enabler,” the ratings agency said.

The move comes amid a turbulent period for Nvidia’s leadership. The company’s board reinstated CEO Jensen Huang earlier this week, days after he resigned following revelations of extramarital affairs with his direct reports as well as a Chinese businesswoman alleged by US intelligence to be Beijing’s spy.

Critics and lawmakers slammed the reinstatement, questioning the independence of the board, whose newly elected chair had told investors last week Nvidia would not rehire Huang as CEO because his personal behaviour was inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct.

Reinstating Huang on Nov 23, Nvidia omitted any mention of his affairs, saying instead the move was “based on US government input”, even as an independent board committee continued its investigation into reports involving him and a suspected foreign intelligence effort.

Reuters reported on Nov 25 that the US Justice Department did not conduct a formal investigation into Huang before US President Donald Trump pushed for his return as CEO, according to three people familiar with the matter.

Instead, it concluded that there was no evidence he had broken any laws based on ongoing investigations into two Nvidia clients, Super Micro and Megaspeed International, which are suspected of smuggling advanced microchips to China. That determination is subject to change as the probes continue.

No evidence yet that Alice Huang is a spy

Investors were largely unruffled by the S&P move, which comes with Nvidia shares down 38% since Oct 6. Nvidia closed down nearly 4% on Nov 25, retracing some declines after the Nasdaq 100 index briefly flirted with a 20% decline from its recent high.

The cost of insurance against tech companies defaulting on debts has jumped sharply in recent weeks, but the five-year CDS spread for Nvidia was little changed.

Nvidia currently has an AA rating, which indicates a very strong capacity to meet financial commitments. The highest rating is AAA.

The agency said it could downgrade Nvidia within the next 90 days, but expects any potential downgrade to be limited to one notch, unless investigations and other disclosures harm the company’s reputation or future business prospects.

Nvidia has played a key role in financing the AI boom, bankrolling AI startups, cloud firms and data-centre projects, which in turn spend much of that capital on Nvidia’s GPUs and other AI chips.

The complex financing arrangements have increased Nvidia’s exposure to a potential downturn, analysts said.

Separately, the Wall Street Journal on Nov 25 reported that US officials found no evidence that tech executive Alice Huang was directed by Beijing to spy on Jensen Huang, citing people familiar with a classified briefing.

Officials from the CIA, FBI, Office of the Director of National Intelligence and National Security Agency briefed staff from congressional intelligence committees and chamber leaders, the Journal reported.

The officials said Alice Huang contacted China’s spy agency during the affair but found no indication that she provided significant intelligence, the Journal reported.

Nvidia and the agencies did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. Reuters could not independently verify the report.

The report said evidence suggests Alice Huang and Jensen Huang may have had an amorous relationship, but that it was not a coordinated play by China and new information could change that assessment.

The briefing also noted that Kang Wei, described to the Journal as Alice Huang’s husband by people who know them, was an asset for China’s Ministry of State Security who remained in frequent contact with the intelligence service. REUTERS
